metadata.title: AASLD Practice Guidance: Diagnosis, Staging, and Management of Hepatocellular Carcinoma
metadata.organization: American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases (AASLD)

epidemiology.incidence: HCC is the most rapidly increasing cause of cancer-related death in the United States

risk_factors.factor: Chronic hepatitis B (HBV) - can develop HCC even without cirrhosis

epidemiology.cirrhosis_prevalence: 80-90% of HCC cases occur in the setting of cirrhosis

recommendation.statement: Adults with cirrhosis should undergo surveillance for HCC using ultrasound, with or without AFP, every 6 months
Patients at high risk of HCC who do not have cirrhosis (e.g., HBV carriers) should undergo surveillance

technical_remarks.remark: Surveillance should not be offered to patients with Child-Pugh C cirrhosis unless they are on the transplant waiting list
MRI or CT should be reserved for patients in whom ultrasound quality is inadequate
AFP has limited sensitivity alone but adds to US for detection

recommendation.statement: Patients at high risk for HCC should be diagnosed with CT or MRI demonstrating hallmark features (arterial phase hyperenhancement with washout)

li_rads.lr4: Probable HCC - requires biopsy or close follow-up
li_rads.lr3: Intermediate - recommend repeat imaging in 3-6 months
li_rads.lr_m: Probable malignancy, not HCC-specific - requires biopsy

pathology.markers: HSP70, GPC3, and glutamine synthetase panel for early HCC diagnosis

biomarkers.afp: Sensitivity of 60% at threshold of 20 ng/mL; not recommended alone for diagnosis

staging.guidance_statement: The BCLC staging should be utilized in the evaluation of patients with HCC

bclc_system.rationale: Only staging system that links tumor burden, liver function, and performance status to treatment allocation

stage.name: A
stage.tumor: Single or 2-3 nodules up to 3 cm

recommendation.statement: Adults with Child's A cirrhosis and resectable T1 or T2 HCC should undergo resection over RFA

guidance_statements.statement: Resection is the treatment of choice for HCC in patients without cirrhosis
Resection favored in patients without clinically significant portal hypertension and Child-Pugh A

technical_remarks.remark: No absolute size cutoff; large tumors can be resected with adequate FLR
Clinically significant portal hypertension: HVPG greater than or equal to 10 or platelets less than 100,000 with splenomegaly
Portal vein embolization can increase contralateral lobe by 20-25%
Laparoscopic resection may offer shorter hospitalization and less decompensation

outcomes.recurrence_predictors: Tumor differentiation, micro/macrovascular invasion, satellite nodules

recommendation.statement: Against routine adjuvant therapy following successful resection or ablation

adjuvant_therapy.evidence: STORM trial showed no benefit of adjuvant sorafenib (RFS 33.3 vs 33.7 months)

recommendation.statement: Observation with follow-up imaging over treatment for patients with cirrhosis awaiting LT with T1 HCC
Bridging to transplant for patients listed within OPTN T2 (Milan) criteria to decrease waitlist dropout
No recommendation for one form of liver-directed therapy over another for bridging
Patients beyond Milan criteria should be considered for LT after successful downstaging to within Milan criteria

liver_transplant.milan_criteria: 1 tumor up to 5 cm, or 2-3 tumors each up to 3 cm
liver_transplant.ucsf_downstaging_criteria: Up to 5 tumors, largest up to 4.5 cm, sum of diameters up to 8 cm

guidance_statements.statement: Transplantation is the treatment of choice for early-stage HCC with clinically significant portal hypertension and/or decompensated cirrhosis
Surveillance for HCC recurrence post-transplant should include abdominal and chest CT

post_transplant_recurrence.risk_factors: AFP greater than 50 ng/mL, poor differentiation, lymphovascular invasion
post_transplant_recurrence.retreat_score: Validates risk stratification from 0 (less than 3% 5-year risk) to 5 (greater than 75% risk)

guidance_statements.statement: Thermal ablation is superior to ethanol injection
Thermal ablation has best efficacy in tumors less than 3 cm
MWA potentially provides better tumoral response than RFA
SBRT is an alternative to thermal ablation, with prospective comparative studies needed
Patients post-ablation are at high risk for recurrence; surveillance with CT/MRI every 3-6 months

rfa.efficacy: Superior to ethanol injection for tumors 2-4 cm
rfa.limitation: Heat-sink effect near major vessels; contraindicated near biliary tree

mwa.advantages: Higher temperatures, shorter treatment time, less heat-sink effect

sbrt.note: Alternative to thermal ablation, comparable dropout rates to RFA/TACE as bridge to LT

recurrence.local_recurrence_risk: Higher with tumors greater than 3 cm

recommendation.statement: LRT over no treatment in adults with cirrhosis and HCC (T2 or T3, no vascular involvement) not candidates for resection or transplant
recommendation.quality_evidence: TACE: Moderate; TARE, TAE, EBRT: Very Low

recommendation.statement: No recommendation for one form of LRT over another

outcomes.improved_patient_selection: Greater than 40 months with DEB-TACE in selected patients

techniques.deb_tace: Drug-eluting beads - no proven OS advantage over conventional

tace.combination_systemic: Phase III trials of TACE plus sorafenib/brivanib showed no benefit over TACE alone

refractoriness.art_score: Assessment for Retreatment with TACE - score greater than 2.5 suggests deferring repeat TACE

tace.guidance_statement: LRT should be considered for intermediate-stage HCC not eligible for curative treatments
Patients ineligible for or progress after TACE/TARE should be considered for systemic therapy

tare.indication: Alternative to TACE for BCLC B, especially large tumors greater than 2 segments with portal vein invasion

versus_sorafenib.sarah_trial: No OS difference vs sorafenib (8.0 vs 9.9 months)
versus_sorafenib.secondary_endpoints: Response rates and tolerability favor TARE

tare.guidance_statement: Current data do not demonstrate benefit of TARE over sorafenib in advanced HCC

recommendation.statement: Systemic therapy over no therapy for patients with Child-Pugh A or well-selected Child-Pugh B with advanced HCC (macrovascular invasion and/or metastatic disease)

sorafenib.adverse_effects: Hand-foot skin reaction, diarrhea, weight loss, hypertension

lenvatinib.note: Expected to become approved option for first-line

regorafenib.indication: After documented radiological progression on sorafenib

cabozantinib.indication: Second-line after progression on prior systemic therapy

guidance_statements.statement: Patients with BCLC B HCC progressing after TACE should be considered for systemic therapy with sorafenib, or lenvatinib upon approval
Patients with BCLC C HCC should be treated with sorafenib, or lenvatinib upon approval, as first-line
Upon progression to sorafenib, regorafenib and nivolumab should be considered as second-line options
Sequential use of multikinase TKIs with similar mechanisms may be considered

multidisciplinary_care.recommendation: HCC patients should be seen in multidisciplinary clinics with dedicated tumor board review whenever feasible
multidisciplinary_care.evidence: Development of true multidisciplinary clinic increased survival

treatment_table.title: Systemic Therapies with Survival Benefit in HCC

stageA.level2: Resection, OLT, RFA, MWA, TARE, TACE, SBRT
